utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. [French on English channel]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Djordjevic is continuing his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Radoicic. We are going to continue from the point where we broke off yesterday. My next question after everything you said yesterday, technically speaking, what was your obligation on the basis of the position you then held in the office of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, previously the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I described it in quite a bit of detail. Technically speaking it meant being in charge of persons who on the basis of establishment were working in the office of the Chief of General Staff in peacetime, and in war time, the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. That meant being in charge of the realisation of all expected and unexpected tasks. Then the use of personnel and equipment and overall resources in the implementation of these tasks. That would be it in the briefest possible terms. If it is necessary for me to go beyond this technical description --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We heard about it yesterday. With regard to this technical aspect of it, we have heard the general aspect, but I'm interested in a specific aspect now. Yesterday you explained that you prepared a certain number of documents, orders, notifications, et cetera. Let us now speak about how mail was received in your office, what preceded the receipt of mail, was it registered, and if so, how, and vice-versa. How did mail from your office go to other units, state organs and so on? Generally speaking, how did this communication develop, did the mail come and go via courier or some other way? Could you please tell us how things went in peacetime and how things went in war time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. In the technological process of organising the receipt -- I mean, I will try to explain the details of this process. So the receipt, review of all the characteristics of the mail concerned because who would be dealing with that mail depended on what kind of mail it was. In the office of the Chief of General Staff, or rather, the Chief of Supreme Command staff, there was a chief of office of the head of office of the Chief of General Staff. Now, that person checked the mail and checked the propriety of the mail received. And I emphasise that. One of the important characteristics involved is whether the mail, as it had previously been reviewed before arriving at the office of the chief of office, whether it had been subjected to the so-called anti-sabotage inspection. If that had been the case, then the person involved in this work was authorised to affix a stamp on that mail, a square stamp saying "PDK," that meant that there were no elements in this mail that could lead to any undesirable effects. PDK meaning anti-sabotage control. Once all of that had been dealt with, the chief of office was duty-bound to hand that mail, all of that mail to the head of office or the deputy head of office, as I was at the time. So that was our duty. Of course, before taking the mail to the head of the office or to myself, he had a log-book of mail received, so that came from the general forwarding service, so they received and sent all mail that arrived, either from Belgrade or from other parts of the country, or from foreign countries. All mail that was being sent to the units and offices of the Army of Yugoslavia. So once the person from the forwarding office would bring this mail for the Chief of General Staff or chief of command staff in war time, we did not receive all the mail, I emphasise that, but only for the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. So that person from the forwarding service had the duty on the basis of this log-book to hand over the mail and then the head of office had to register all the mail he received in the log-book of his office. As I said a few moments ago, he had to review it after handing it over to the head of office or to me as a deputy head of office. He actually had to categorise the mail received and then to register who he was forwarding it to further. My job was on the basis of visible features on the mail concerned -- there were -- there was also an open kind of mail, if I can put it that way, telegrams. So I had to deal with whatever the mail was. If it was urgent, then I had to deal with it urgently. If it was urgent for the Chief of the Supreme Command staff, then it would immediately be handed over to him. So that was the process of receiving mail in that part of the staff of the Chief of General Staff. If you are interested in further activities carried out by myself and the head of staff, I can explain that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When the Chief of the General Staff would receive mail from his associates, primarily his own Chief of Staff or deputy Chief of Staff, what measures were taken and what kind of obligations did you then have?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after receiving the mail and familiarising ourselves with that mail that we then handed over to the Chief of General Staff, we were either asked by him personally to stay at his office to see what kind of mail or document this was so that action could be taken immediately, quite literally on the basis of that mail, or if five or ten minutes were required, not more than that, then we could wait in front of his office and then he would call us back in, and he would give us orders either in writing or orally about what should be done with that mail. I repeat, if the mail was urgent, so throughout the aggression, regardless whether it was day are or night, we received from him orders either on the document itself, rather, the description of our duties in terms of how we should act upon that mail on the basis of his having looked into the content of that mail, or he would attach a piece of paper to that mail saying what he had to say on the basis of the significance of the mail concerned. Then on the basis of his position stated on the document itself or on this attached additional document, we knew very clearly what we should do further. If the mail was a report or a request or whatever, there were many different types of documents, so in that report it was usually command reports or requests from subordinate commands. Then on this attached document or on the margin of the document itself, he would state his views, and then it was quite clear to us what should be done further, whether it should be sent to one organ or several organs of the Supreme Command staff or strategic groups, or perhaps we should be addressing some of the state organs, the federal government or particular ministry or several organs. Each and every time he presented his position very clearly, immediately, so the chief of the office and I were very rarely faced with a dilemma as to what we should do with a document. Once we would be given these tasks, then the head of office or I would process the document technically, and our duty was to hand that over to the chief of that office that was in charge of distributing that mail, or rather, sending it to the appropriate organ or ministry concerned. All of that was part of that process of receiving and distributing mail, and it was based on instructions that had previously been adopted, so it was very clear for all how mail could be traced. I think that I've been quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: One of my questions was in what way did mail leave your office? Was there just one way, or was there a number of ways depending, for instance, on the secrecy, the importance, confidentiality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was precisely my duty. I will try to be very brief, but for laymen, it may look simple, although the entire procedure is very complex. Anyway, I'll try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but this is going to be very important for our later understanding of certain things that you will be explaining in the process of our Defence case, but please try to make it understandable for laymen.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a document had to be delivered to one of the assistants of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff or a representative of any of the agencies that were located together with the Supreme Command staff in this special facility, which was our base at the time, after technical processing which meant formatting, retyping, in keeping with the position stated by the Chief of the Supreme Command staff, that document would be logged. That was compulsory. If it had a regular number 250-1, then after our logging, it would become 250-2. That was done in the filing department. If it was to be delivered within the same location, then it would be simply handed in personally by our office manager or his deputy within the premises of the Supreme Command staff. If it had to be delivered to someone outside the base of the Supreme Command staff, then an authorised representative of the central forwarding service would be called in and they were located not in the same place as the Supreme Command staff, but in the vicinity. That person would come to take over the mail because the central forwarding service had well-established organisation, had the technical means, and facilities to deliver mail throughout the territory of Serbia. So that person from the forwarding service would receive the mail, sign for receiving it in our log-book, and then that would be the end of that part of the process. And I also have to emphasise that on that document even there would be an indication of urgency such as very urgent, or defence, strictly confidential, or military secret strictly confidential. There was a place for that indication on the envelope and the authorised person from the forwarding service would have a very clear indication of what procedure was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, after this explanation, I would like to know what kind of log-books you had, what kind of registers, and how you archived your documents.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Log-books are a prescribed type of document, and they exist even today within the system of correspondence in the defence system, which includes the army and the defence ministry. On the very forms that are printed on each page, on the left page and the right page, and in the way they are bound, they provide for a very precise and clear overview of the entire procedure, any document goes through, be it a document of the highest level of secrecy, state secret, or military secret. So that book has the left side and the right side. On the left side you would see the entire procedure of handling the document by the sender and the addressee. On the right-hand side, however, you would see further action taken upon the document. So the author of this log-book designed this in a very purposeful and practical way. It has proven to be a book that provides for security and clarity. You can see immediately what was sent, what was received, who it was received by, what it was done with it later. Every step in the process of handling with all time indications for every step. The log-book makes it easy even for a layman to understand, the entire process of handling and distribution while proper concern is given to secrecy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in archiving, was there a possibility for a document to be received by the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff without being logged? And if that happened at all, when would that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I will try to be as brief as possible. All documentation that the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command received was not received exclusively from our office, but perhaps 90 per cent went through us because he was well aware of the importance of the technical processing of the documentation according to proper procedure. However, in exceptional cases, one of his immediate associates or assistants who were constantly in touch with him would bring directly to him a document that had been received by their organ, and after consultation with the Chief of the Supreme Command staff, the chief would always make a decision what to do with it so that there would be no loose ends. He would invite the chief of his office or me and tell us to log the document as received, and that action would be taken in a way that he would indicate either on the margins or on a separate piece of paper, as I described earlier. Anyway, that circle had to be closed so that everyone would know what to do with the document afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about archiving?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Archiving became topical only after the end of the aggression. The Chief of the Supreme Command staff immediately after the aggression ended issued to the entire army and all the related organs, all the organs associated with the Supreme Command staff with a central order that was very almost perfectly precise indicating what had to be done with all the documentation that had been received or sent immediately, all the correspondence from the beginning until the end of the aggression. Everything was prescribed very clearly and every chief of every organ had a clearly prescribed procedure to follow including dead-lines. So everyone in this defence system knew what he had to do in the process of preparing documents for archiving because this is a very complex process, from initial review, initial inspection, to check whether all the properties of the document meet the requirements, to checking whether all the action necessary had been taken upon a document, in that if this action had not been completed, then archiving had to be postponed. Or perhaps, the document had to be deferred and archived with an indication that action upon it had not been completed. All these instructions were contained in this central order which was very comprehensive but not so comprehensive to be completely sufficient, but in any way, everyone knew what to do in order to carry out this procedure properly, because it was a very serious and very complex task.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My last question in this set of questions --

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, in that order, in addition to those people who had to deal with the preparation, it was very clearly said and agreed what the military archives had to do. They had a plan which told the archives at what time they would be receiving a representative of which organ with their documentation, and then that included inspection, whether the documentation was properly processed and whether all the requirements for receipt by the archives had been met.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Last time you mentioned -- many times you mentioned rules and you said these things were prescribed and this was a time-tested process. My question is, was there a bylaw or a rule book on office management in those situations, not only in terms of archiving, but also in terms of log-book and office administration?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say the army and the defence system, I mean the Ministry of Defence itself as an agency of the state and the entire state system, and they prescribed every aspect of the functioning of the defence system. How, where, and when, those were the pillars of the state. At that time in Yugoslavia and later in the union of Serbia and Montenegro, as everywhere in the civilised world, the system of defence closely monitored all these procedures, so the Army of Yugoslavia did not function all by itself. They followed the general administrative proceedings as prescribed and they applied to all state organs. Everything that was written in the law on state administration and the bylaws concerning office administration, and that was applicable to the defence system was applied. These were not any idiosyncratic special rules, apart from the rules concerning dead-lines because our documents were sometimes marked military secret, and they had a limitation on safekeeping that had to be observed by the archives. All the rules on administration and handling were the same as for civilian authorities. There were the same laws, bylaws, and decisions of the defence authorities, various determinations and orders, all these regulated the office administration in the army and defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned weekly and monthly plans at the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. During the war, what did that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the complexity of our work in peacetime and war time, and when I say "our work," I mean the whole system of the armed forces, in view of all that complexity much earlier when the first plans began to be used in our system of work in the army planning became a very important function because the implementation of every task could be optimised by planning. We tried to place everything within a planned framework and thus we created weekly and monthly plans. There was an annual plan that lay as a basis for these. These plans were discussed and adopted at the sessions of the collegium of the chief of office -- sorry, the Chief of the General Staff in peacetime and Supreme Command staff in war time, and during the war we also tried to work in a planned manner, not chaotically, and as we made weekly and monthly plans, but also daily plans because our duties multiplied to such an extent that it would have been impossible to work without a plan. But we tried to reflect all our weekly and monthly duties in these plans to facilitate their realisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In war time, was there an establishment body that was hired in the Supreme Command staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire defence system envisaged that in case of a state of war or a state of emergency partial or complete, there was the highest organ of the state managing the entire system of the state, and it was called the Supreme Defence Council. That was the highest body at the top of that pyramid conditionally speaking. The Supreme Defence Council. And the first body in the defence system subordinated to that highest body was the Supreme Command staff. I suppose you know about the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly. But I want to ask you, during the war in 1999, what kind of communication was there between your office and this body, the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything about that communication was prescribed and regulated, and it worked like this: The Chief of the Supreme Command staff, because the Chief of Staff always had his own office in peacetime and war time, and in war time it was called the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. In war time also, the president had his military office. That office was headed by the head of the military office, and the Chief of the Supreme Command staff also had his head of office. So if there were some assignments or duties that emanated from a position taken by the president or the Chief of the Supreme Command staff, and if they had decided that communication should be relegated to the interoffice level, then we would do so, we would organise communication between the president's military office and the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, the Supreme Command staff, during the war, was it in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, or was it in Belgrade all the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual seat of the Supreme Command staff was at the command post of the Supreme Command staff in war time, and that meant in the Belgrade garrison. I say that intentionally, the seat. The function of the Supreme Command staff implied that it would function throughout the territory as required by all the tasks placed before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The head of staff of the Chief of Supreme Command staff was who?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Milan Vlajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You were deputy?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was deputy head of office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, to what extent, if any, did the scope of his responsibilities differ from yours?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our scope of responsibility differed in terms of the actual responsibility involved. Colonel Vlajkovic was the person with top responsibility, and he had the highest degree of authority in terms of the unimpeded functioning of the entire office. That was in his hands. According to internal regulations that stipulated the rules governing everyone's work within that office, he had the obligation and duty to convey certain duties to his deputy. So the responsibilities of the deputy differed to a small degree from the responsibilities that he had. That was the rules in peacetime and in war time. But if you remember, I said yesterday that our tasks and responsibilities grew at such a rate that the two of us really did not look into all of that, who had more powers in which particular field. We simply tried to share the workload. We acted with full responsibility anyway and we thought we should share the workload.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, ex officio or in some other way, did you attend meetings of the Supreme Command staff, and if so, what role did you play in that context?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have the authority to attend if the head of office was away on official business, then it was my right and duty, of course, to attend these sessions. Our overall activities, I mean, mine and Colonel Vlajkovic's, meant that it was only once or twice that Colonel Vlajkovic was prevented from personally attending that session or such a session, so once or twice I attended sessions of the collegium. Some people call them briefings, other people call them sessions, but officially the name was sessions of the collegium of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. They were held every day. Sometimes when what was happening in the territory of the entire country required it, then even two daily sessions were held. At any rate, they were held once a day usually in the afternoon or in the early evening. I underline that because after these sessions people got very busy. They had to act on the basis of the tasks issued at those sessions. When I participated in these sessions, or rather, when I attended them, it was my duty, just like Colonel Vlajkovic's, to have minutes written up and to record in brief terms what happened at the session so that after the session we could technically process together with the other organs of the Supreme Command staff the tasks that were invariably set at these sessions. Of course, it was the Chief of the Supreme Command staff that issued these tasks. He received proposals from different organs but at the end of the session, he was the one who would draw the appropriate conclusions and set the tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the -- it was the head of staff who was particularly duty-bound to attend these sessions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Ex officio, it was the head of staff, the chief of office, rather, of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff who was supposed to attend these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: During the aggression against the FRY, did you know the accused police General Vlastimir Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a citizen and as a person who was within the defence system, I just know of him from the media and from official reports. However, I did not know General Djordjevic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you ever have a document leave your office and go to Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic, or rather, to the position that he held then, head of public security either personally or, as I said, simply to his office, to the particular office holder that he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally never had occasion to see any such document or to personally take part in the processing of such a document, or did the chief of office ever inform me of the existence of any such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic then held the office of the head of public security of the MUP of Serbia, and did you ever receive any official mail from him at the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such thing, and I personally have never seen or received any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My last question within this particular set is whether you personally had any knowledge during the NATO aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia about the alleged ethnic cleansing or persecution of Siptars, or rather, Kosovo Albanians by our organs? When I say "organs," I'm referring either to the military or the police or both the army and the police, and if so, could you please explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I move on to my next set of questions, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to allow the usher to give the witness a binder with written exhibits that will be shown to him in order to facilitate the proceedings because very often the copies are not perfectly clear when displayed on the monitor. This is what we did in previous cases as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radoicic, could you please look at document number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Otherwise, could we have on our screens document D008-1213. I beg your pardon, D008-1053. In the binder it is number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radoicic, could you please look at this document and explain to us, or rather, could you first tell us whether you know of this document, whether you've ever seen it. And if that is the case, could you explain to us within your answer what kind of document this is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen this document several times. The first time when the document itself was created, that is to say, at the time when its processing was completed within my duties as an authorised official in the office of the Chief of Staff. And the second time was when before this same court there was another defence case going on and then now again, so I'm saying, yes, I know this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have your comments today with regard to this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a document, of course this is a copy, is called "Archive List" and as such, it constituted a document, or rather, a form that military archives provided to all responsible persons within responsible organs of the Supreme Command staff who had the duty on the basis of the order I mentioned a few moments ago and the process of preparing documentation for military archives. So this is a form that was and still is called the archive list. It has different sections, and when a party was submitting such a request, then they had certain obligations and then the party receiving it had certain obligations too. Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please stop at this point. From the OTP we received a document also called "Archive List," D008-1713 is the number of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to tender this document, I mean, the one that we've just seen. The one that we've just seen I'd like to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a document with any particular relevance to this case, or is it being tendered simply as an example?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The question that will follow after the question that I will put now will pertain to both archive lists, so perhaps we can wait for that to happen and then I'm going to tender both documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it would be wiser if we did it that way so that it would be clear to the Trial Chamber what the intention of the Defence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So, please have a look at this document. It seems to me that the number of the document is identical, if I'm not mistaken. In your binder that is number 9 probably. No, sorry, 7. It should be 7.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no number 9. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: 7. Or if you cannot find it, just look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not on the screen, it's still the archive list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it's a different document, that's why I'm asking you. This is a document provided to us by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that is on the screen is number 1 in the binder. Number 7 is the log-book here in the binder. I've just found it. It's number 6. 6.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just found it, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please compare the two documents.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard for me to carry out an appropriate comparison. In this binder under number 1 in the upper left-hand corner I can barely see the degree confidentiality and the date. I can perhaps make an assumption as to the date on the basis of some of this other information that is barely legible. And now this other document that was shown to me that is number 6 in the binder, it is very clear that it is document 400-6. The date is the 10th of August, 1999. However, in this document I cannot see what the content is. Now, was that done intentionally? There's this column, Title and brief description of contents of archive unit. Was this redacted on purpose when it was copied? Quite simply we cannot know what is written there. It's only on page 7 that we can see. So on pages 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 respectively of this archive list that you showed me now at this later stage, it is only number -- page number 7 starting with number 79 that has a title and brief description of the contents of the document. Here it is. That is the difference that I managed to notice. So in my view, it is not equally visible and you cannot see --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the stamp what can you conclude?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see the stamp of the -- which one do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This one at the top in the right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the left-hand corner is the logging stamp or seal, as it should be called, of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. And in the right-hand corner is something that is printed as part of the format. It looks like a seal, but it isn't. The receiving party in this case, the military archive, assigns a reference number under which the document was received, the date of receipt, and in these appropriate boxes they write how many documents and how many sheets in total are contained. On the document you've shown me, all this information is visible in the first copy you've shown me and in the second one. The difference between the previous one and the current one, as far as this part is concerned, on the first page, is that on the previous one, there is a stamp of the military archive in the right-hand top corner, whereas on this one there is no such stamp. Why it is missing, I really don't know. These are briefly my observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could we now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we are not able to grasp what is being explained. Are the two documents that are on our screen the two documents being compared by the witness, or does he have some other document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm comparing a Defence exhibit with a Prosecution exhibit contained in their notification. So we are trying to establish whether this is indeed the same document with the appearance slightly changed because on the Prosecution copy one part is not visible, maybe because the paper was placed on top of the document during photocopying. I just wanted to clarify this because I believe -- you see the inventory number, 21606 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, could you just stop and listen. We have on our screens two documents. One is an original. It may be a copy of an original. The other is a typed English translation. Now, the witness seems to be talking about some different document from the one we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I understand, Your Honour, what the confusion is about. Here on the screen we have a document, the original, and the English translation. What was shown to the witness previously was a -- I will give you the number of the proposed exhibit and I'll ask the usher to place it on the screen. D008-1053 in Serbian next to the document D008-1017, also in Serbian or B/C/S, so we can compare these two original pages. That was my question. You see the B/C/S on the right-hand side, it says "Archive List," but this is document D008-1053, and on the left-hand side, we have a document proposed by the OTP and the number is - just a moment - D008-1713. So these are two documents. Now, we see the reference stamp on both. We see the contents of the third column on one of them but not on the other. That's what I wanted to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more difference to point out. One of these has the military archive stamp, and the other doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Which one has it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one you called D008-1053. In the right-hand top corner where it says inventory number, it also has the military archive stamp. And the one on the left-hand side, it has the stamp of the office, but not -- no, no, please, let me draw your attention to this. Both documents normally in the left top corner say the same thing, the Supreme Command staff, et cetera, although legibility is not equally good. However, the document on the right has the same inventory number, but one of them has a round stamp of the military archives in the right top corner, and the one, the other one you showed me, D008-1713 does not have that stamp in the right top corner. So to me as a connoisseur of this business, it is quite clear that it is the same document but from two different points of processing. From two different times, two different stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this is enough. I will move to my next question. Could we now place on the screen D008-1017, both the B/C/S and the English versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think in your binder it's number 2.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We are waiting. Here it is. You see it on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen this one before, this is the third time I'm seeing it. This is a letter from the retired army general, Mr. Dragoljub Ojdanic, that he addressed to the chief of office personally, chief of the office of the Federal Defence Ministry, and at that time yours truly was occupying that position. May I continue? He addressed this letter to me with a kind of urgent appeal and he is pressing me to receive documents that he had requested earlier. And in this letter, in addition to the urgency of the request, he also expresses his personal dissatisfaction over my attitude to his request addressed earlier referring to the same issue. I received this. It was officially logged at the office of the federal defence minister in March 2002, which happens to be my 51st birthday, and I was frankly surprised by his comments addressed to me personally. At first, I thought he was sending me a card, and I was really surprised by some of his even insulting remarks, but he was expressing some justified dissatisfaction because he had expected a quicker response.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, so that we can understand why this letter was addressed to you, let's have on the screen P888.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, it's number 3, I think. All right. You see the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the document preceding this letter by General Ojdanic written on your 51st birthday, as you said? First of all, do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not contemporaneously, but I know about it from my evidence in Milutinovic when I was shown the document. I know it from that time, and this is the second time I see it. But during my tenure and on this date, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you comment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can comment --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: From the technical viewpoint?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the technical features, I can't understand. Normally documents that are marked military secret, state defence, and strictly confidential always have to be numbered because it's either a state secret, very important, or military secret strictly confidential, also very important, which must have an indication of how many copies were made and are distributed under specific numbers to a limited number of persons. This number is missing. That's my first comment on the technical aspect. Second, I can't understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the second page before the witness continues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 2, I don't see that the creator of this document and the sender of this document indicated, as he should have, to whom it was delivered and what action was taken further. If it's addressed -- well, I believe that people who are familiar with this technique know very well the difference between addressing something and delivering something. Those are two different things. The sender did address the letter. It could have been addressed to me or to the United Nations or I don't know who, but the address is there. Here at the end it doesn't say delivered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom to the left we see some kind of stamp.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where to the left?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, below the signature of the commander, colonel-general, I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my document under tab number 3 there's no such thing. Anyway, it doesn't say to whom it was delivered. Just let me finish. If it's delivered to just one person, it has to say "delivered to" at the top, and the second line would read "files" or "archives" otherwise we couldn't trace it. It is prescribed by the rules that the sender has to indicate to whom his correspondence was delivered. Nobody cares to whom he addressed it. Copy number 1 to one institution, copy number 2 to another institution, et cetera. This sender could have also sent -- have sent this to the Supreme Defence Council for their information, but it's not indicated. Nothing is indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We see something in the right-hand corner on the monitor. We need to see clearly the number in the right top corner, it begins with a 7, but there's something else. Now we see it. What does this number 72 mean? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no clue. At the office of the Supreme Command staff, such handling of documents is not allowed. So this must have come from somebody in the military archives or somebody who handled the document or, I don't know, I can only guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now we have the same problem that we had as we did with the archive list. This same document, except that now the document has some other markings on it as well, was received from the OTP. So could we please have the first page of the document submitted by the OTP, that is 3D10-0057. Could we have the first page of the original of that document, the B/C/S version, placed right next to the B/C/S version of this document that we now have on the screen. 6038 is the 65 ter number. Could you lower it a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this now. Is it the same text? Is it the same organ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have it in the binder, or is it only on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that it should be under number 4 in your binder. So first tell me whether you can recognise the text as being the same or not as was the case with the archive list a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see on the screen, it is one in the same text. The same form of processing. This does not have the number of copies in which it was made. Before you asked me about number 72, but as opposed to that, this document has number 248, and I also have no idea where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about this seal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has a stamp that I cannot see, but I can only assume --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only see some letters, so I'm just making an assumption. If it's the military archive, then I see OJ, and I can see the coat of arms. But the copy of this document is almost useless. We see something that resembles the stamp of the military archive though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is this down here that we see starting with a Y and then it says Y0252272? What's that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see it. It is not characteristic of any kind of action that is taken at the office of the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we have both pages right next to one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I be reminded which document has which exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the right-hand side, Your Honour, is 3D10-0057. And the one on the left-hand side is P888. On the left is P88 -- it's part of the Defence notification, and the one on the right-hand side is part of the Prosecution notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The number you are giving, could I point out, Mr. Djordjevic, 3D10-0057 is the number in the Milutinovic case. In this case, the same document is 65 ter 6038.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6038. I've already said that once, I'm sorry. But once I saw with regard to this document it is -- I see that the transcript does not reflect what I said. It is 5888 [as interpreted] so it's three 8s. Could both be scrolled up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that preceded by a 5 or a P?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P, a P.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the document on the right. 6038 is its 65 ter number. We see that there is one extra stamp on the left-hand side. Can you give us your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You won't mind, but I keep distinguishing between a stamp as in "pecat" and a stamp as in "stambilj."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not very knowledgeable about that kind of thing. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess that this is a professional deformity on my part, so I make a fine distinction between the two. So this stamp says the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Supreme Command staff, the office of the chief, Strictly Confidential Number 248-2, the 26th of May, 1999. What I truly cannot understand is how come two documents can circulate whereas one does have a marking to the effect that someone had received it, and the other one does not have that marking? So this stamp of the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff could be placed subsequently, but I'm saying I see these two together for the first time, how is it possible for the same a document to be circulating in two different versions in terms of processing? I mean, there can be a stamp here that it's was received at the Hague Tribunal as well, for instance.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There can be different kinds of processing, but I've already said that I did not see these two this way before, so I do not understand how come this happened. I have to add one more thing that is very noticeable. Perhaps if somebody else has this kind of a professional deformity in terms of a high degree of perception in this respect, the first document had the signature of the sending party, and then in the left-hand part there was a signature with a stamp, the command of the 3rd Army with the coat of arms of Yugoslavia, how is it possible that on this other document this stamp has a different position as it were and a different slant in terms of how it was stamped? And it also doesn't say how many copies were made. So it's either someone who is not very well versed or someone who is not responsible or someone who is not authorised to act. I don't know what to call that person. If this was done only two copies, then it is possible to have these two differences, or rather two places stamped in a different way, but if it was done only in one single copy, if there's just one original, then how can a photocopy be made and differ from the original? Because we see these details here on the screen, and I can see it in my binder. It is quite obvious, it is glaringly obvious that these are documents that within a certain period of time were handled subsequently by certain persons with a certain intention. Probably today for some reason one can go to a particular place and ask to have this kind of seal affixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would this be a convenient moment to take a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you one more thing. The signature is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tender documents because I have a number of questions left before I tender this document because I would like the Trial Chamber to understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it the proposition of the Defence that the contents of this -- these two documents differ, or merely that there are the differences that have been explained so far by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The contents are absolutely identical. However, the differences are in the accompanying stamps or seals, "pecat" or "stambilj" as the witness says because I really am not knowledgeable enough to make that kind of a fine distinction in terms of stamps, but there are differences in terms of registrations and numbers, and we'll go back to the archive list as well so that I can explain to the witness why I asked to have an explanation of what this archive list was and then I'm going to tender both. You saw that the archive lists are the same, they have the same numbers, however one has an extra stamp and then some numbers differ, and I think that ultimately it is going to be perfectly clear to one and all once we reach the end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, may I make another important observation in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the date, I see that here on the stamp it says the 26th of May, and the document was processed on the 25th of May. So if we are talking about urgency, if the Chief of the Supreme Command staff should be familiarised with this urgently, then the document had to say "urgent," "very urgent," or if this cannot be sent as a telegram by teleprinter, if it had to be sent by courier, then it would have to say "urgent" or "very urgent" on the document itself. Very urgent meant that if the territory so permitted, it would be done within the course of the same day, and urgent meant by tomorrow at the latest. And it would have to state that it's compulsory sent by courier. So in order for this document to reach the Supreme Command staff from the command to the 3rd Army within such a short period of time it had to be sent by courier or by teleprinter. There was no third option. It doesn't say how urgent it is and also it was not sent by telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How come you know it wasn't sent by telegram?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, I could break at this point because the next point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The last answer was not heard, the last answer of the witness, because you and the witness are overlapping in your haste.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I so apologise. I was quiet while he was giving his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So let us repeat it. You said that the document, the document that you explained, or rather, the last thing that you said, could you repeat it once again, and I shall wait patiently.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequently I asked you to give an important remark in my view, something that I noticed subsequently as I looked at it, namely, if the document was processed on the 25th of May, and this is the first time that I see that it was received on the 26th of May, I see on that stamp. So if we are talking about such a brief period of time, this kind of important document in terms of its content could have been sent in addition to the shortcoming that I referred to originally, it doesn't say in how many copies it was made. It also has no marking as to whether it's urgent or very urgent. Then further on, I explained if it's very urgent then it had to be dispatched within the same day, and if the idea was to have it received within the course of the same day then it had to be marked that it should be sent by courier. To this day, there is a stamp, an auxiliary stamp precisely for these purposes in all military units and in all organs of the Ministry of Defence and of the army, this stamp is placed on a document and on it it says "urgent" or "very urgent." And underneath that it says "deliver by courier." On this document, which in terms of its importance and in terms of the speed, according to which it should be delivered, there is no marking as to whether it's urgent, very urgent, or whether it should be delivered by courier, and it is certain that it was not delivered by telegram or as a telegram because the document does not contain the characteristics of a telegram. Perhaps I did not quite identically put it as I did the first time, but that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 5 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to address something before the witness comes in, if that would be all right with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Because there's a little confusion with some of the documents that are being discussed with this witness, I thought it might be helpful if I give the Court a little contextual information and it may make some of the testimony make more sense. With regard to two exhibits, which it may be helpful if the Court just had. I have hard copies of them that you can have before you when I say this so you know what I'm referring to. With regard to Defence 65 ter 638, and Defence 65 ter 644, if the usher could just bring that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are these documents which have been put to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, these were the two archive lists that the witness was comparing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The numbers you just quoted are not the ones that seem to have been used at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm using the 65 ter number. I think the Defence is using a document ID number which I do not necessarily have all of their document ID numbers. 638 is D008-1053, and 644 is D008-1713. These are basically -- they are two copies of an archive list from this witness's office to the archives, to the military archives, and this first copy, which is Defence 65 ter 638, which looks like this, if Your Honours can see, this one, this was presented by the Ojdanic Defence in Milutinovic, and they obtained it from the government of Serbia. This is a copy obtained from the archives, and it's an excerpt of this list. So because it's a copy, it has this stamp from the archives here that it's a copy from the archives, and it's a shorter excerpt. And later the Ojdanic Defence requested a full colour copy of the original, and so that's what this other list that the witness was comparing, that is what 65 ter 644 is. The Ojdanic Defence then got this colorful copy of the list, so it doesn't have the copy stamp up here, and it's longer. It's not an excerpt and the archives, or someone, redacted out some of the content because apparently they didn't want that to be given. So that is the source of these two documents there. The same thing, they are just -- one is an excerpt form and a copy and the other in full form and not a copy. And the other two documents that were being compared are P888, this 25th May letter from 1999, and 65 ter 06038, which is the same 25th of May letter, but it has on the back page a stamp from the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff, and it also has another stamp on the front. And P888 was received by the Prosecution in the Milutinovic case from the government of Serbia, and 06038 is another Milutinovic exhibit. That one was received by the Ojdanic Defence, and they were asked on the record where they got that document, and they said that they received it from the National Council for Co-operation. So these are documents that those received from different sources. Possibly that can give the Chamber some context so when you hear these documents referred to you will have that background information. I believe with the archives which I spoke of first, it seems that this witness may not be aware of that so he may not be able to speak to it. However, this information about the source of these was contained in the Milutinovic testimony of Mladenovski, who I believe is on the Defence's list of witness, so if the Chamber has further questions he may be someone that you can address. So hopefully that can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radoicic, let's pick up where we left off. We still have the document on our screens, the one that we have been discussing previously. My next question is, since we already heard from you that during war operations you had not had an opportunity to see such a document, assuming that this kind of document has reached the office of the Chief of General Staff or the Supreme Command, what was the presumed procedure and what would follow thereafter? Let's say that this is our working assumption just as I gave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my earlier statement, I described in general terms the procedure applicable to all documents, and what kind of methodology was implemented by the chief of supreme staff and his office. This kind of document or report, first of all, if it had arrived from the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army, or rather, its forward command post, as it is stated in the letter, received special treatment for the reason that in this area, all the combat operations were at their highest. And in comparison to all other documents and reports, arriving from the area of the responsibility of the 3rd Army were given, I have to say extremely pronounced importance and was given highest priority in processing them. So if this kind of report would reach the location where the Supreme Command staff was, and especially if it was addressed to the Chief of Staff of Supreme Command, then the responsible personnel from the chief's office would deliver this document to him directly in the fastest possible way. When I say "in the fastest possible way," means that if the Chief of Staff at the moment when he is in receipt of such an important document, was somewhere outside the very headquarters of the Supreme Command, then this important document would deserve to be delivered to him as soon as possible and literally we will resort to a procedure of urgent delivery to his hands directly wherever he is. If he was in the seat of the Supreme Command, he would receive it immediately. However, if he was outside of the seat of the Supreme Command staff, he would also receive it within the shortest possible term. I'm positive, and I say with full responsibility that he, the chief of supreme staff immediately after being informed about such important issues contained in these documents would write his instructions on the document itself indicating who and when is obliged to continue to act upon this document. From the content of this document, one can see that this kind of document would definitely warrant, based on his assessment, immediate distribution of the document to the members of the staff of Supreme Command, and I'm sure certain state organs as well because this has to do with the resubordination of MUP units as it is stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you this: In view of the time that you spent alongside the Chief of Supreme Command and Colonel Vlajkovic, who was chief of office of the Chief of the Supreme Command, and you said that you spent quite a lot of time with him, do you remember that there was information to the effect that you acted on the content that is contained in this document, and would you remember such an occurrence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would definitely remember that. As far as I can remember concerning this particular document, I did not take any action because I didn't have a chance to see it while the aggression was in progress. But let me ask you, and first of all, I would ask the Trial Chamber to tell them that during the break I - I felt some kind of anxiety, first of all because I have given a solemn declaration, and throughout my career I only made one oath and that is when I joined the army in which I pledged that I was going to abide by everything contained in that oath. When I appeared before this court for the first time, I also gave a solemn declaration to speak the truth, and as a lawyer, I am personally interested in committing to do everything as long as I live for things to be proven and preserved. I'm really upset, maybe you can feel it in my voice, that there are two types of documents in circulation that the processing methodology of these documents give rise to a high degree of anxiety in me, and I wonder if something happened with these documents in terms of the tampering or being abused. So for the sake of truth or untruth, some people are incarcerated and some other people are free. As a human being and as a lawyer I think it is my duty to do my best not to deprive someone of their freedom by addressing all these issues responsibly. So by looking at this document, it seems that somebody has received this document but only subsequently, and somebody is trying to prove something with that, then the truth must be completely different. And I would really like to emphasise that this gives me rise for concern and anxiety that the truth is being treated in this and that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have again Defence Exhibit Number D008-1053.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's number 1 in your binder, Mr. Radoicic. We have both versions in B/C/S and English, and could you please show us the last page of this document where we have the seal and two signatures. Can the witness please tell us who signed this archive list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if you can please zoom in on the signature and the seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see only one signature on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature because I was the only authorised person to do that. That's why you have this note on the left that I personally put, and it says, P over O which stands for by authority of the chief of office, Colonel Vlajkovic Milovan, who gave me this authority, and that was my working task in processing the documents for the military archive, and, therefore, I signed this document. And only the seal could be put on my signature and the signature of Mr. Vlajkovic. Other persons were not entitled to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please now look to the left and see who has compiled this list.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see here that this list was compiled by Miodrag Jankovic, but his signature both on the screen and on the hard copy is almost invisible. You can see just two or three lines, no more than that. Therefore, I cannot say definitely whether it was him who signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please look at the document itself. We have that there were some corrections and additions made in this document, in the original. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I don't have the original here, all I have are some rather illegible copies, but as far as I can discern, in column 7 it says, Received on behalf of the military archive warrant officer 1st Class Dusan Mladenovski and this is probably his signature, so this is no one from the office who signed this but rather this warrant officer from the military archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But this column that has a register number, who added these things in writing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at page 8, these are corrections probably made by this warrant officer or the responsible person from the archive, that is what he did at the moment when he received the documents. So during the hand-over they literally checked all the numbers and all the elements relating to the documents that were being handed over, and this warrant officer Mladenovski probably for the reasons known only to him, probably by complying with some regulations, he made some additions. In one place on this page, page 8, I see that actually he made more than one correction, but it is very legible, as if this were a financial document. He did cross out certain entries, but you can still see what was stricken out. So he did it properly, and one can see what was before and what was added subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the previous page, and that's page 7 in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at entry 82, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Official Note of the meeting between the Chief of Supreme Command staff and the chief of administration for the preparation of the republican organs for defence in the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Ministry of Defence." Do I have to repeat it slowly?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Official Note of the meeting between the Chief of Supreme Command staff and the chief of administration for the preparation of the republican organs for defence in the Republic of Serbia of the Federal Ministry of Defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from Yugoslav Army there were other organs who were responsible for Defence under the Law on Defence. I hope that you know that we had two laws. The Law on Defence as the broadest legal instrument that governed all defence issues in the then Yugoslavia, and the Law on the Army which governed only the issues relating to the army. Since in addition to army there were other organs responsible for the tasks and obligations relating to the defence system, there were a few of them, and amongst them was an organ which was called, Administration for the preparation of the republican organ in Serbia, and the same organ existed in Montenegro. Both of them were under the jurisdiction of the Federal Ministry of Defence. In peacetime the Chief of General Staff didn't have any jurisdiction over the activities of these two organs. However, during war since the whole functioning and the regulation of the whole defence system is unified, and as I said at the very beginning, involving units and organs of the Yugoslav Army and that of Ministry of Defence, all of them were in war time under a unified command which was called the Supreme Command. So for that reason, the Chief of Supreme Command had the right and the authority to regulate certain activities of these organs as well in the given circumstances. For that reason, probably this Official Note was drafted, and it was necessary to draft it because they definitely discussed certain tasks that these administration organs were obliged to carry out. For example, to take care of the functioning of transportation, traffic, railway transportation, communication system, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So for us to understand everything that has been done so far, can I please have next to this page 7 B/C/S version of 65 ter 6038.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We shall see that in this original there is something written that is closely related to what we have been discussing so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can you -- yes, that's right, we need to see the stamp and the seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We can see here in this document in the upper right corner the number 248, and we have a seal for which you assume that this is the archive seal, but if we look on the left side under item 82 in this archive list, we see number 248-1, and underneath somebody wrote 248-2. Then in the next column we see that somebody crossed some numbers by hand and added new numbers. Since you signed this document, did you enter these corrections and what is -- what do these corrections signify?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier when I was explaining this document to you I said that I put my signature on this document after the responsible person from the office of the Chief of General Staff compiled this list and confirmed that it was ready for hand-over. That means that it contained all the entries, numbers, description, register numbers, and all these boxes that needed to be filled. But this was not done by us as the ones who were handing over the document. All these documents were done at the moment when the hand-over took place. So present during the hand-over was the responsible person from the handing over party, and also the responsible person from the receiving party, in this case, the archive. The only person authorised to carry out these corrections was the representative, or rather, the authorise person from the archive. We were never allowed to enter any corrections ourselves. So all these corrections that you see in this document were done actually, I suppose, by this warrant officer Mladenovski as a recipient responsible person. While I'm answering your question, I'm looking at these correction that is entered under number 82, I can't help but notice that the handwriting under 82 of this correction is not identical, or at least it doesn't look identical to me, to the handwriting of the only person authorised to make corrections, that is the person from the archive. It seems to me that this was written by someone else who I don't think was authorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What does this 248-1 and 248-2 mean in this entry number 82?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing is striked. It was just added in this column log number below 248-1, it was just added, 248-2. And in the columns number of documents and number of sheets, corrections were indeed made 2 and 5 were written instead of 1 and 3 respectively. That means there were two documents instead of one and five sheets instead of three.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back to page 1 and to the stamp. I just -- we just need to change the left side. D008-1023. Sorry, 1053. We need to see the first page. Let's see the stamp on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It says here, Number of document 277, and sheets 735. That's in the stamp. Now if this correction was made and rubricated too, does that mean that the number documents would have to match if we add up the documents and sheets, should the final result be as written here, 277 documents containing a total of 735 sheets? Should that be so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I understood you were saying, but I told both you and in the previous Defence case, this is not a stamp, it's part of the formatting, and these boxes are envisaged and printed there to be filled in. As to your question, you are absolutely correct. From what I can see, the handwriting of this authorised official from the military archive indicates that there were 277 documents, no correction added; 735 sheets, no correction added. And it's quite certain that at the end after receipt, you should have counted the documents and the sheets and written the correct number. It's up to that authorised official. He should do this in a responsible manner. Anything else would be forgery, it would amount to forgery and tampering.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, next to this -- my last question about the relationship between these two documents, does the document on the right, 248, we see that it completely correlates with the archive list, does that number have anything to do with this first document, and in what cases would a number be placed on the document as an addition under the rules?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number added subsequently, 248-2 with a basic number 248-1, this number 248-2 is the number of some follow-up document that should be related to the basic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would there be an obligation to state what document it is about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perfectly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We see only one document indicated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that person indicates two documents but does not specify what the other document is. You had an opportunity to see what the log-book looks like. 248 is the basic number, and everything that follows, which is called subnumber, dash 1, dash 2, dash 3 or 4 must be correlated with a basic number. So if 248-1 is the basic document and refers to the minutes from this meeting, all the follow-up documents, dash 2, dash 3, et cetera should relate to that document that those minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After this, the Defence will tender, and I give my thanks to my learned friend from the Prosecution who took the trouble to give us additional information about the sources of these documents, I will tender, as I said, D008-1053, which is the archive list we've just seen, but also the other one, D008-1713, also archive list which we established would be the same document but redacted, some of the information is concealed. And we also tender 65 ter 6038. It's the number given by the Prosecution, and the exhibit number is P888, but it's related to the previous three exhibits, and that's why I want the previous three documents to be admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit, the one which is D008-1053 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00583.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the other archive list, D008-1713 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00584, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the relationship of these two documents with P888, we have another document 65 ter 6038. It's identical to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 65 ter 6038 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00585, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have got to tender D008-1017. That's a request or an application by the already retired Chief of the Supreme Command staff to this witness, and it's P888. And we also tender D008-1017, the letter by General Ojdanic sent to the federal Defence ministry, to the attention of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00586, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now call up D008-1109. D008-1059.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's number 5, Mr. Radoicic. Would you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
