utterances.text: It's the log-book, and it's bound in such a way that sheets cannot be taken out. Otherwise it would be punched and have a special guarantee string running through it. It's written on the cover that it's the log-book, but this is the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is that book for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You enter or register or more precisely file all the documents that deserve to be registered in the log-book of the agency keeping the log-book in keeping with its purpose. This is the log-book of the chief of office of the Chief of Staff of the military command, and it's marked to indicate that there is only one book which means that it contains the proper record of all the documents that were designated by the rules as deserving to be entered into this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up something that's already been exhibited. But before that, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I are forgot to say one important thing, namely, on this page we also see the stamp of the military archives, which I suppose means that the military archives must have received all the documentation logged here because they affixed a stamp. Or perhaps the military archive was duty-bound to place this log-book at somebody's disposal, if they were so required.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I tender this document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00587, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up D008-1729.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's number 7. Is it the same document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At face value I would say it's the same document. I mean, the same page because it's not a document, it's a page. Except that the one you are showing me now does not bear the stamp of the military archive, whereas the other one did. And one thing escapes me, what does this number 1 mean? This 1 was written there by someone for reasons only they knew, because to me to put it informally it looks like scribbling. So somebody with no authority scrawled this 1. An unauthorised person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would it be allowed to make subsequent corrections?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This log-book was treated in the same way as financial documents, meaning that it was not allowed to take out any sheets or tear anything out. And any correction wherever would have had to be marked as a correction. Who could have made corrections and at what time? If the correction was made while the log-book was still operational, running, that correction would have to be explained, and the explanation would have to be indicated in a proper rubric or column, that is, in one of the vertical or horizontal boxes, if there was any room to make a correction there under the same number. If there was no room, then an Official Note could be written up describing what was done and for what reasons, for what justified reasons, and that correction would have to be reflected in that Official Note, and the Official Note would have to be attached to the page where it -- to which it pertained. And it would then not be allowed to separate that Official Note from the page in question. It would certainly not be allowed to use this white paint you call corrector or fix-it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I emphasised, I don't know if you were paying attention, it would certainly not allowed to make these corrections on the part of the sender. Now, later when it was already in the hands of the archive, I don't know what approach they took and what actions they were allowed to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another witness who will be speaking about that, I'm only interested in the part that concerns you and the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. So this document D008-1729 is hereby tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00588, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go back to D008-587 [as interpreter]. That's document that has already been admitted, the previous document. Could we please have a look at page 54, I believe it's the second page in terms of what was submitted. D008-7059 was the number actually. Just a moment, please. It's the second page, isn't it? So could we have page 54.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D587 for the transcript. I see that it has not been recorded correctly. Could you please zoom in on 248.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about this? Obviously it is P888, that's already been admitted into evidence under that number. So you see 248, so it's the log-book of the Chief of General Staff, his office. It says number 2 --

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what number is that in the binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We haven't got it in the binder. You can look on your screen. It can be seen very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that a few moments ago I had on my screen the original of the page with the original colour of the ink and stamp and now I see this other thing where it says 248. I can barely discern, so there's a difference between me saying I can see or I can barely discern. So is this, to strictly confidential S.POV, the 26th of May, 1999, and as far as I can discern in the column where it's 15th of May, 1999, it says, SMO dash -- I'm barely discerning what is says there, I can barely barely discern this, I think it says [B/C/S spoken] administration. But I don't know what the rest says. As opposed to that first entry, the other one on the 26th of May, 11 days later that is, says KDA 3rd commander, IKM, and it says that the sending party sent it 872-94/1-2. I mean, it says here slash 1-2, but that does not look like what documents should be marked like with all propriety. So I can see this second entry very clearly, I mean, the handwriting, but not the first one. And I don't understand why not. And also, this basic number where there is a reference to the sending party, namely the Ministry of Defence, it says, Command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any logic there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the point of view of everything that I have tried to explain to you so far, with regard to the prescribed procedure and the powers and authority in keeping records and registers, this does not look like proper record keeping. If I can take the liberty of saying this, it looks like something that was subsequently entered. It either has to do with someone's ill intentions or ignorance. I believe that the responsible person who was in charge of doing this could or should never have done any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We have the right person to ask about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I personally within the discharge of my regular duties in war and in peace supervised everything single day and provided guide-lines, that was part of my job, to the work of the office at the office of the Chief of General Staff in peacetime and also in war time, and it could never happen that -- I mean, there would hardly be a day that would go by, I mean, I'm not talking about working hours I'm talking about days because often we worked all day, so hardly a day would go by without me looking at books. This kind of thing would not have happened without me knowing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me once again, you saw the first document, we cannot even see what it says.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just allow me to say one more thing. So what was done under this basic number two completely different documents from two different fields were put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can that be done?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last topic that I would like to deal with is P1505. Could I please have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to admit to you that this was really unskillfully done. I mean, no matter how hard some person tried --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1505, please. Thank you. Could we have the English version as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's number 8, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document, please have a look. I would like to clarify this matter. I don't want it to remain undiscussed, and we do know of its existence in evidence. So again we are talking about resubordination of MUP units. Again we are talking about the command of the 3rd Army, again with your talking about General Nebojsa Pavkovic, you will see that when we look at page 2 of the document, however, what you have before you is a hard copy so you are already seeing this, but could you please give us your comment on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is scope for making comments in terms of the quality and technical aspect involved, and also the content involved and also the structure of the content as far as I can see as I glance at it diagonally. There is scope for both types of comments, technical and substantial. With regard to page 2 of this document as well. So first of all, it says on page 2, a telegram can be sent. So my first technical observation is that if this was sent as a telegram, then it had to have as an integral part a copy of the technical processing of this document. Although it is marked as a telegram, it is a document, or rather, what is marked here is the intention of the sending party to send this as a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just interrupt you for a moment, and can we just show page 2 now for the benefit of our colleagues from the OTP. So please wait for a moment for page 2 to appear on the monitor. Not everything can be seen now so could you please adjust the page accordingly. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Radoicic, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that we have page 2 here as well, first of all, we cannot see that it's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not marked that it is page 2 in relation to page 1, so this in its own right can be a page that continues on to another text. It doesn't say that it's page 2 of this document at all. That's my first observation. Secondly, if an authorised official like the Chief of Staff, and over here there is a mistake, it doesn't say Chief of Staff, instead of a B, there is a V, so maybe it's a typo. There should be a signature by the said person here because he was authorised by the commander that it says here that this can be sent as a telegram. So the assumption is that say the commander dictated to him over the telephone, but he is authorised to act further on in accordance with this document that it can be sent as a telegram as it says here, so if he did send it, he had to sign it because the commander who had issued the order, or whatever page 1 says, is absent, so in his absence it is this person who is authorised to sign the document for him so that the document can be sent as a telegram, so the commander, I mean or rather the person processing the document had to say commander, Colonel-General Nebojsa Pavkovic S.R. that means on behalf of, for, signed for, so this other page -- this page does not have S.R., and it doesn't have the signature of this other person who is authorised to order the teleprinter operator to send this as a telegram. What I started saying a moment ago when you interrupted me was that there is no evidence of this document being sent as a telegram. This is typed out on a computer. When a document is being sent as a telegram you probably had occasion to see what it looks like, what it looks like when you are sending a document by a telegraph. So it does not contain any proof of that here. There should be a signature of the authorised official here that it was sent as a document. Had it been sent as a telegram, it would have to say who it was delivered to, so the teleprinter operator on the basis of the regulations regulating the work of teleprinter operators, state that once a telegram is sent on the -- or rather, I'm sorry, in the lower left-hand corner he has to leave a stamp, the teleprinter operator, when he received it, when he sent it, and when the receiving party received it. So there is no trace of all of these actions that are prescribed. Without that, this document is just a piece of paper, although it does have up here a seal that I can barely see. While I tried to explain at first in terms of how documents should be treated when they are state secrets, military secrets, strictly confidential, et cetera, it doesn't say what number it is. This is a strictly confidential document. I glanced at its content, and it certainly could have had a higher degree of confidentiality because it involves a large number of organs in the defence system and also state organs as well, so it doesn't say how many copies, it doesn't say, therefore, which particular number this copy is, the one that we see now, and in relation to the breadth of the issue that is being dealt with by the author of this text because if it were the sending party then it would be marked as a document that is being sent, and there is not a single marking that this was sent let alone received elsewhere. So the author, the creator of this text did not deal with that. There is no number as to what copy this is. So if he had the intention to send this, instead of sending it to the Chief of Staff at the Supreme Command, he is sending it to the sector for KoV. So I don't understand what his reasons were to address it to the sector of the KoV.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is important is whether you remember since you held the position you held at the Supreme Command staff, do you remember this document? Did you see this document during the war, the document you are looking at now, either as a telegram or in this form?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, in the briefest possible term, I had no occasion to see this, I did not see it. I deeply believe that this kind of document was never received. As I've already said, it has no markings in that sense that it had been received and I mean, it hasn't even been marked by their teleprinter operator, let alone that it was received at the Chief of Staff at his office, I must point out paragraph 8 is so important that this must -- this would have to reach the Chief of General Staff or had it reached the Chief of General Staff, he would have to inform the head of the VSO about it. There is a reference here to a certain Levic and then also to Djindjic and Vesna Pesic and Velimir Ilic, Veli Ilic. So these are systems -- persons outside the defence system, so it is certain that if the Chief of General Staff had received it this, the president of the Supreme Defence Council would have to receive that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who would work on these documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either the office or one of the organs of the Supreme Defence Council because there's so many questions here, look at 10, shortage of ammunition, the assistant chief of the -- the assistant commander for logistics would have to deal with this. And also say communications, again by the appropriate assistant commander in that field. Then number 8, paragraph number 8, this would certainly call for action on the part of the information administration, the security administration, one of the assistant commanders and also the position of the Chief of General Staff would have to be sent to the president of the Supreme Defence Council, either through the military office or the president of the Supreme Defence Council would be aware of this, or at regular meetings, the Chief of the Supreme Command staff himself would at a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council make the president aware of that. So that would be say paragraph number 6 local electronic media. Again the administration for communications, then another paragraph, the appropriate administration that was supposed to regulate matters related to conscripts who were mobilised, then also other matters related to the Supreme Defence Council, was it the president of the Supreme Defence Council or the president of Serbia who would have to look into this kind of conduct by representatives of the MUP. Then number 2, privileged position of the members of the MUP under quotations marks. So 1, 2, 3. Important questions are being raised here with regard to the activity of the MUP. So this is such a comprehensive document that the Chief of General Staff would have to have an extraordinary meeting of his collegium to deal with all these important matters. And of course, he would also urgently familiarise the head of the Supreme Defence Council about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Had that been done, what you discussed just now, could it have happened without you having no knowledge of it whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm stating to you with full responsibility that I had no opportunity to see any such thing, and I do not remember seeing any such thing. There is not a single piece of information that would jog my memory in the sense of my having seen this earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would thus conclude my direct questions for the witness, and I would like to thank you Mr. Radoicic for having devoted his time to us so that we would all work in the interest of justice. Thank you. Let me not forget, can I tender this document. Oh, no, actually it has been admitted. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to make sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I just would like to make sure I understand a few things about the position you had during the period of the NATO bombing. In paragraph 3 of your statement you say that you prepared almost all documents sent to the military office of the president of the FRY. Who would these document have been from, and I don't need an extensive -- was it just documents from your office, or was it from other organs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that we, I'm referring to the entire office, not only to myself personally, when we wrote to the military office of the president of the Republic of Yugoslavia, or rather, in war time, the president of the Supreme Defence Council, that could have been only, and I'm emphasising this through my words and my tone of voice, it could have only been on the basis of the positions taken by the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. And when the Chief of the Supreme Command staff would decide that the president of the Supreme Defence Council should be made aware of certain information, then it could only be sent that way with the signature of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. If he personally was the author of a particular document and stated his position, and if he would sign that document and then he would give me, that is me and the -- and Colonel Vlajkovic I'm saying we in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm only asking if the documents that you prepared were from the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command or if other organs, you were preparing documents from other organs. That's all I need to know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot go into the entire history of the creation of these documents for the following reasons: The Chief of the Supreme Command staff was made aware of certain things in different ways, in writing or orally. So all organs that had an obligation towards the Chief of the Supreme Command staff sent written information to him or informed him orally. As for the military office of the president of the Supreme Defence Council, it's only the Chief of the Supreme Command staff who could directly address him, not someone else. Not anyone else for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You stated that after the evening briefings, you worked with the chief of the office to process and distribute tasks. I just want to understand what you mean by that. Do you mean that when the tasks would come from the evening briefing you would process them into written tasks and distribute those to the people who were to do the tasks? Were these tasks in writing, that's my question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are only interested specifically in whether they were in writing, then the answer is yes, but I can also explain to you the technology involved in these tasks, but that really depends on your interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Just to clarify your answers, they were in writing and then those written tasks were distributed to the people who were to do them; would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have understood that very well. These tasks were written up, logged, registered in log-books, in books of records, and submitted in a proper way to all organs who were supposed to act on the basis of those tasks during the course of that day. Of course this procedure of sending and receiving was also recorded from the organ who was sending it to the organ receiving it. So a document always had a closed circle. A document could not start moving without its entire movement being recorded. It's not that it would start in some way and then no one could see how it was finalised. That simply could not happen. One of my obligations was not to allow through my own work or through my supervision of -- over the work of others that this be in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I believe you stated today that you attended the evening briefings yourself one or two times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And did you attend any other meetings with General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such meetings and discussions. When I say "meetings," that means involving two or more persons. There were also talks with one person only and on such occasions, he would ask me or Colonel Vlajkovic to come in order to take notes or to leave a written record of that conversation if it so merited.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So of the meetings that General Ojdanic had in the office where people would come in to meet with him or out of the office where he would go out to meet with other people, would you usually go with him, or was this something that you only did sometimes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I or Colonel Vlajkovic went with him on those occasions and to those places when he deemed it necessary. We did not go regularly. He knew that we were busy enough as it was in the implementation of the other tasks that we had, he highly respected the time involved for carrying out these tasks and the obligations we all had. He didn't really mind about that kind of thing. He was really very caring in that respect. It was just important that a person who would be a note-taker would accompany him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. I think it's time for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the second break now. Resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, if someone else attended a meeting with General Ojdanic as a note-taker, was it part of your job responsibility when those notes came back to review all those notes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other duties, it was also the duty of the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command to look at such documents, and he would mandatorily indicate his position on such documents or he would invite us personally to tell us his position and what to do with the document. How to dispose of it or whether to archive it if no further action was required. But it would certainly have to be logged.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Are you talking about documents or the notes? I'm asking you about the notes taken by a note-taker at a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every meeting had its form and if notes were taken, notes are also official, at least in our understanding and jargon so notes were also an official document. And the very copy book in which the authorised person wrote down bullet points or took notes about the activity concerned, was an official document. The copy book itself was an official document. And if a separate sheet of paper was used, that separate sheet of paper was also an official document. So notes were also a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And did you personally review all those notes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was the person who was entrusted with that, yes, but it would be either the chief of the office or myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So did you -- I'm trying to find out if you did or not. Did you regularly do that, or was that not something that you regularly did?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Now, you explained in your -- when you were being questioned earlier that when documents came into your office, they got logged.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 645. Okay. I'm sorry, I guess I failed to note that this has already been admitted. It's 588. D588.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, is this the log of your office where you logged -- where the office logged all of the documents that are received?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said already in my evidence that this is the first page after the cover of something that should be a log-book, is supposed to be a log-book. So I don't know if this is log-book. This is just the first sheet in what is supposed to be a log-book and in the form that I see on the screen --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could just look at one more page, perhaps that would help.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So, sir, is this the log-book for all the documents that were received in the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can see are two pages of one sheet in this log-book. And what we see on the screen is a copy of the original of that book, in fact, a scan of these pages, and if we could just zoom in a bit. Perfect. Maybe zoom out a little now. So this is a scan of the original, and on these pages we see what the Defence counsel asked me about a moment ago. This document 248 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And for now I just wanted to confirm, so we are clear, that this the log-book. We'll come back to this in a bit, and I'll ask you a little more about it, but right now I just wanted to confirm that's what that was. If we could now --

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I just have to intervene --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, sir, we'll come back to this, and just for the sake of time, we don't need to -- you gave a very good explanation in your other testimony and so I have some specific questions later, but for now if we could just move to D584.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would really like to be given an chance to say that I want.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, the only question put to you is whether this was the log-book of your office. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you asked me if it is the log-book. You asked me if it was that log-book, and that's what I wanted to say. These are pages from the log-book, but I am -- can't say that those are the pages of that log-book. They are pages in a log-book of the kind that is kept at the office. I don't know which pages they are or whether it's that log-book, the cover of which you've shown me. Those are two separate things, and that's why I thought I should point it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, sir, is this a log of documents received in the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What? Which? What we see on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: No, the document we were looking at before that you were still giving an answer about.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now looking at this document, this is, and you spoke about this before, this is the archive list of documents from the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff that were taken over to the military archives. Sir, were all of the documents that came into your office archived, or were some not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All documents, if you remember from my previous evidence, all documents action upon which was completed from the period to which the order for the archiving of documentation during the aggression pertained, all documents upon which action was completed were thereupon archived.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope you understand when I say completed. If I need to explain why, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: If we look in column 4 - and if we could scroll up the exhibit a little - I've noticed that it appears that numbers are skipped, if we were to look at -- this pattern follows on other pages also, but here if you notice it goes from 135 to 137 and without going on I would represent to you if you look at other pages, it's the same thing, not every number is included in the log number, so I just was wondering, does that mean that certain documents were not archived, or can you explain why some numbers are skipped?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That follows up on where I stopped in my previous answer. Documents were turned over only if action upon them was completed. And in that basic order where the Chief of the Supreme Command staff prescribed to perfection which documents had to be turned over to the archives, it was stated that those documents upon which action is completed should be prepared and turned over to the archives. And those documents upon which action was spending. If for, some instances they concerned material damage incurred during the NATO aggression and the amount of damage had to be established and claims had to be settled, these documents were not turned over because action was still pending, and some of these have still not been completed. And those documents were not turned over to the military archive. And those documents that were not archived were the subject of reports prepared by every organisational unit in the Supreme Command staff. And that's how you get the sequence of number skipping a few. Only by comparing log-books and identifying the numbers missing can you understand the substance of my comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. So if we were to look through this, through the pages of this, we've seen, as you can see on this first page, there are handwritten amendments to this archive list, and I think you stated in your direct examination that these were not made in your office. So would you agree that it appears that at the archive unit, errors were discovered and corrected by hand on this list?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person in charge at the military archive made these modifications and additions with certain justified reasons. I could not arrogate the right to give you an objective comment of all these reasons that were guiding that person, but I know for sure that this authorised person from the military archive would not allow themselves to make an addition or modification without any justified reason, including the Law on the State Military Archive of which -- on which I'm not an expert, as well as reasons that the military archive found in the same order, because that order did not apply only to the Supreme Command staff but it also specified the obligations concerning appropriate procedure for receipt of documents by the state military archive. This is all I can tell you in answer to this question. But that these additions were made by someone other than the authorised official, that should not happen. So I believe that somebody did this in a perfectly appropriate way because he left visible marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. I'd like to now move on to the letters between you and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could first look at D586, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, in this letter General Ojdanic asks you to look into whether the office of the chief of the office of -- the chief of the office of the Chief of the General Staff, if you had received these two letters or documents from General Pavkovic, the 25th of May document and the 4th of June document. And in this letter he refers to you, if we look at the second paragraph of the text of the letter, he says: "I urgently remind you to fulfill your official obligation to me, which in no way a private one, in your capacity as chief of the office of the Chief of General Staff of the VJ." Now, during the time of the NATO bombing, that wasn't correct, right, you were the deputy chief of office; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. This appeal from him without this reference to the second paragraph is completely justified.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in the second paragraph if we look at the entire chronology --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm only -- all I want to know is if this is inaccurate that he referred to you as the chief of the office when you were, in fact, the deputy chief of office? Is that right, that you were not the chief of office as he referred to you in this letter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you that he personally recognised his own mistake. It was an honest mistake because at that time I was deputy chief and not the chief. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at your letter in response to him, which is -- I don't believe this has been used yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: It's 65 ter D -- 65 ter 633, it's D008-1015.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we look at the third paragraph of the text of your letter, you say: "With regard to your second letter, your reminder which I received on 11 March 2002, I have no knowledge for the reasons stated above (because I was not chief of office at the time) that any such report was ever sent to the Chief of General Staff of the VJ." It seems that you are saying in the letter that you don't know whether that report was received because you weren't chief of office; is that what you're saying in the letter? And we'll look at the next sentence also, but were you saying you didn't have personal knowledge because you were not chief of the office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I did not put this in the best way. Among other things, I did not know anything about this also for the reasons indicated in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And if we look at the next sentence it says: "In addition, a check shows that such documents have not been recorded in the register of the office of the VJ, Chief of the General Staff." Correct? That's what you've put in that letter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I can explain further, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, are you stating that it wasn't in the log, that you asked someone to check and they checked the registry and it wasn't in that log that we've seen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we go to D585, which is this letter in question that we are talking about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you wanting this tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, can I please tender that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01528, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And if we look at the second page of this down at the bottom of the page, on the left-hand bottom corner, is that a stamp that shows that something is received by your office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a stamp from the Supreme Command staff, office of the chief. So it's the stamp of the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff, but I cannot confirm that it was received. What I can see is an authentic stamp of the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. Whether the handwriting and the rest are really those of the authorised official, I cannot know because this does not verify delivery by someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: What does it mean? Does it mean -- I was understanding that it meant that it was received by your office, but is that an incorrect understanding?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not an incorrect understanding. I know that there is a prescribed procedure and if it were followed, this document should not be -- have been treated in this way. However, the stamp could have been affixed later. I cannot exclude that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And setting aside at this moment whether it's possible someone could have done it later, this is the stamp of your office, though; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you, it looks to me like it is. This is a copy of a copy, but this corresponds to the form of the stamp of the office of the Chief of the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that it looks like it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And if we look back at Exhibit D584. No, I'm sorry, I need the registry, D587. And if we could go to the second page. Oh, I wanted the one that is the original. It should be -- it was 645. I'm sorry, 588. And if we can just zoom in a little bit, and we don't need the English. I think we're a little more concerned about what the original -- the scan of the original looks like here. If we could just look at the line closely that says -- for the document that says 248.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, setting aside, I realise, sir, that you have certain questions about this line, but on its face does this line in the log-book log that this document was received, if we compare the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, we don't need to look back at the other document, but I'd submit to you that the letter we've been speaking about is Strictly Confidential Number 872941-2, and if we look at this line 248, does this appear to log that a document with that strictly confidential number was received by your office on the 26th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the face of it, it looks like it was logged, and that means received. But it also looks to me like something written subsequently, at a later date, not only subsequently, but incorrectly or inappropriately. Obviously with some ulterior motive, the person made this entry subsequently, at a later stage, because the basic document, 248-1, relates to the administration for the preparation of defence organs. And it's incomparable, these are unrelated things and even a layman would not have made such a notorious mistake to place a document that has to do with the army and a strategic group in the same column of something that relates to organs of the Ministry of Defence. And me as a stick in the mud professional, it is obvious even from the ink that this was added later. Everything is written in italics in this second line and much more legible than the first line. The document with dash 2 is from a completely different opera. It's like putting fruit and vegetables in the shop window of a jewellery store. These things do not go together, but it all depends on the intentions of whoever wrote this, and they could have had bad intentions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could not have been done like this in my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you look at the first line in 247 and compare the handwriting where it appears that the same thing has been written in column, I believe that's column 4, doesn't the handwriting in 247 look to be the same handwriting as in 248?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say it was not the same handwriting. It's evident that the author is the same. The handwriting is either similar or the same. I didn't say it was a different handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now going into something that looks like graphological expertise, and neither the witness nor my learned friend are experts in the field. So I think I am justified to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I remember several passages of his evidence in chief, Mr. Djordjevic, in which he expressed views where the handwriting was of a particular person or not. We are well aware that this witness doesn't claim to be a handwriting expert, but his evidence is given on that basis. Thank you, Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, sir, I guess you've stated that it appears that the entry for 248-2 was written in later, but it would have been written in later than the line above it because that document was received on the 15th of May; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either you were not interpreted correctly or perhaps you misspoke. Chronologically viewed, the date 15 May is earlier than 26 May, so the 26th of May could not have come before.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I was asking -- you stated that the handwriting for the entry for the document 248-2, which has a date of the 26th of May, you said that it was written later. I am assuming you meant later than the document one line above it. And my question to you was, it would be written later, correct, because the date for that document above it was earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You stated in your examination-in-chief that you were never aware of General Ojdanic - I hope I'm saying this right - being part of any plans for ethnic cleansing. And I think in your statement at paragraph 14 you stated that you don't know of any plans for ethnic cleansing of Albanians in that paragraph also, or you've never seen General Ojdanic in your presence urge anyone to commit war crimes. But, sir, we have established today that you did not accompany General Ojdanic for many of his meetings, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just asked two questions. Which one am I supposed to answer? Two or more questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, the question to you is, we've established that you didn't accompany General Ojdanic to many of his meetings, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered that. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So you only would have known of such plans if they were included in a written task or written notes that were then archived in these books, in these logs; is that correct? These notebooks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If there were plans to do such a thing, do you agree it probably would not be written down in official documents and tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation, but I understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, would you like me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. You can ask that question rightly only of the person who was the author of such activities. I cannot make any assumptions. I was only involved in processing documentation in keeping with the verbal instructions I received.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I don't have any more questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Djordjevic actually, for the interpreter. I do not have any redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe I did do my best at addressing you correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know that that concludes the questions for you. The Chamber would want to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague and for the attention and assistance that you have been able to give to us. You may, of course, return to your normal activities now. And a Court Officer will show you out. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems no point in commencing a further witness at this hour, unless you have an urgent need to do so. Is there any matter that needs to be raised by either party?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had announced that I had a matter to raise but given the time, I would prefer to raise it first thing tomorrow morning before we commence with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you can remind us of that tomorrow morning, Ms. Kravetz, we'll --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of February, 2010,at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.
